stem: A client with a pelvic malignancy describes pain that travels down one leg as 'burning, shooting, and like electric shocks,' with intermittent tingling. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: The pain qualities suggest a neuropathic component related to nerve involvement and warrant focused neurologic and pain assessment.
options.B: The pain is most characteristic of uncomplicated visceral nociceptive pain because neuropathic pain is usually described only as a dull ache.
options.C: The description rules out cancer-related pain because nerve-related pain does not occur from tumor involvement or cancer treatment.
options.D: The pain quality is clinically unimportant; only the numeric pain score should guide further assessment and management.

rationale: Neuropathic pain results from injury or dysfunction of the peripheral or central nervous system. NCI identifies tumor infiltration or compression of nerves and treatment-related nerve injury as important cancer-related causes. Burning, shooting, pins-and-needles, and electric-shock-like qualities are characteristic clues to a neuropathic pain mechanism. Pain assessment should include quality, distribution, neurologic symptoms, intensity, function, and contributing factors; the numeric score alone is insufficient. Recognizing a neuropathic component helps guide further evaluation and an individualized pain-management plan.
educational_objective: Use pain quality and associated neurologic symptoms to recognize a neuropathic component of cancer-related pain and trigger focused assessment rather than relying on pain intensity alone.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health; National Library of Medicine/NCBI StatPearls
source_version_date: NCI Cancer Pain PDQ current 2026; StatPearls current 2026 resource accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NCI Cancer Pain PDQ — pain classification and neuropathic pain section; StatPearls Pain Assessment — distinction between nociceptive and neuropathic pain based on pain quality
source_claim_supported: NCI defines neuropathic pain as pain from peripheral or central nervous-system damage and identifies tumor nerve-root involvement and treatment-related injury as cancer-related causes. NCBI identifies burning, shooting, pins-and-needles, and electric-shock-like qualities as suggestive of neuropathic pain.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation — assessment and management of alterations in physiological function, including pain and neurologic complications
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition and assessment of neuropathic cancer pain
correction_summary: Rebuilt the original descriptor-recognition item into an applied cancer-pain assessment scenario. Removed the inaccurate implication that nociceptive pain is uniformly dull and aching, added tumor-related nerve involvement as a plausible cancer mechanism, and required focused neurologic/pain assessment rather than rote labeling. The final item avoids prescribing a universal drug regimen because treatment depends on etiology, severity, comorbidities, and the individualized plan.
audit_findings: Original item correctly identified neuropathic descriptors but oversimplified nociceptive pain as essentially one dull/aching phenotype.

Fresh NCI and NCBI review supports burning, shooting, pins-and-needles and electric-shock qualities as neuropathic clues and identifies tumor or treatment-related nerve injury as relevant cancer mechanisms.
The final scenario requires interpretation plus focused assessment rather than a vocabulary-only response.
No universal analgesic recommendation is embedded because neuropathic cancer-pain treatment is individualized and may be multimodal.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct interpretation with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, unsupported pain-classification claim, or unresolved source conflict.
